stories.author: antoniomika
stories.title: Running coding agents without handing them my credentials
stories.groq_label: A specialized set of tools allows remote AI coding agents to perform tasks without directly receiving sensitive user credentials.
stories.groq_explain:
Antonio developed a security tool called lend to allow remote AI coding agents to access local credentials and tools safely. In his development workflow, he runs multiple AI coding agents in parallel on remote, disposable virtual machines while keeping his sensitive credentials, SSH keys, 1Password vault, and logged-in command line tools strictly on his local laptop. The lend tool bridges the gap by allowing remote agents to ask the laptop to execute specific commands or sign SSH requests on their behalf without giving the agents direct access to sensitive tokens.

To manage parallel agents across virtual machines, Antonio uses herdr, a custom terminal multiplexer built for AI coding workflows. Herdr tracks whether agents are active, waiting, or completed, and allows agents to start and monitor other agents. He pairs this with Ovis, a web and mobile interface for herdr that turns terminal sessions into chat threads and sends push notifications to his phone when an agent needs input or permission.

The primary problem lend solves is credential exposure on remote hosts. Standard approaches to remote authentication involve either copying API tokens onto the remote machine, where any process can read them, or using SSH agent forwarding, which allows unrecorded key signing and only works for SSH. With lend, a proxy sits in front of the local SSH agent on the laptop. Remote virtual machines communicate with lend over a forwarded socket using an SSH agent extension to request command execution or key signature operations.

Requests sent through lend are verified against a local JSON policy file on the laptop. The policy defaults to denying all requests unless explicitly allowed by rules that define permissible binary paths, subcommand argument prefixes, and required approval methods. Approvals are typically tied to macOS Touch ID prompts. When a remote agent needs to run a command, lend displays a request dialog on the laptop showing the full executable path, arguments, working directory, and agent-provided justification. Once approved via Touch ID, the command executes locally on the laptop, and stdout, stderr, and exit codes stream back to the remote agent, ensuring secret keys and API tokens never leave the local machine.

stories.author: mfiguiere
stories.title: Why 3dfx 1 cards had such a washed out color output?
stories.groq_label: 3dfx 1 cards produced washed out colors because their linear hardware color output mismatched textures created for non-linear displays.
stories.groq_explain:
This content addresses why 3dfx Voodoo 1 graphics cards produced a washed-out color output during the late 1990s. John Carmack explains that both NeXT and 3dfx tried to implement linear color spaces intentionally, drawing from professional graphics backgrounds at Pixar and SGI. In a linear color system, pixel values correspond directly to photon emission levels, allowing straightforward math for blending, filtering, and texture interpolation. 

Linear color systems work well when a display system supports high bit depths of ten or more bits per color channel. However, 3dfx cards only operated at five or six bits per channel. Human vision does not register brightness linearly; human eyes perceive relative changes in light intensity and are much more sensitive to subtle differences in dark tones than bright tones. Spreading a low number of available bit values evenly across a linear scale creates noticeable intensity banding in dark areas and wastes visual precision on bright tones.

The primary cause of the washed-out visual appearance was that digital artists created game textures on standard non-linear displays. When 3dfx hardware rendered these non-linear textures under its linear assumptions without applying mathematical gamma correction, the output appeared faded and washed out. Game developers at the time were captivated by the raw rendering performance of 3dfx hardware and did not fully understand display gamma management during the glQuake era. 

This issue matters because gamma handling across textures and render targets remains a tricky aspect of computer graphics. While high display resolutions and 24-bit color depth mask most gamma errors today, improper color space management can still cause subtle visual artifacts like edge shimmering in modern games.

stories.author: kristjansson
stories.title: Optimizely compromised, served malware on Zoom, GitLab
stories.groq_label: Compromised Optimizely snippets delivered malicious JavaScript to hundreds of major sites, enabling crypto theft and data skimming.
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports a large‑scale supply‑chain attack that occurred on 16 November 2026, in which malicious JavaScript was delivered to visitors of 178 well‑known websites through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. Affected sites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France‑KLM, Ledger and Peacock. The malicious code was a multi‑purpose malware kit that performed cryptocurrency address substitution, payment‑card skimming, cookie theft, screenshot capture and, on iPhones and iPads, delivery of the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits. At least some cryptocurrency was already stolen, as evidenced by verified transactions to the attackers’ wallets.

Optimizely Web works by having each customer load a JavaScript snippet from Optimizely’s CDN. The snippet contains Optimizely’s core code, the customer’s experiment definitions and an optional “Project JavaScript” field where customers can insert custom code. The attacker injected malicious code into the Project JavaScript of many unrelated customer projects while leaving the rest of the snippet unchanged. Because the snippet continued to be served from the trusted cdn.optimizely.com domain, browsers accepted it without raising alarms.

Three variants of the injected loader were observed. Most snippets included a plain script tag that loaded a remote file from https://1688360.cc/track.js. Some variants hid the same URL in base64 and decoded it with atob(), making a simple search for the domain ineffective. A third version embedded the payload inline and executed it via eval if the remote URL was blocked. The attacker also re‑infected sites that had previously been cleaned, indicating continued access to the Optimizely project. Some customers hosted the snippet on their own domains (for example opt.scheels.com or www.vodafone.com.au); those copies were compromised as well because they originated from the same Optimizely project.

The article does not know how the attacker obtained write access to so many distinct customer projects. Possible explanations include a breach of Optimizely’s own systems, compromised credentials with cross‑customer privileges, or another unknown method. Optimizely’s CDN merely delivered the content it received, so the attack was not a CDN cache‑poisoning incident. Optimizely’s own sites (www.optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com) were also affected.

A detailed timeline shows the progression from earlier injections on Turkish sites in September, through the registration of the attacker’s domains, to the first Optimizely injection seen on the BBC snippet, the modification of Zoom’s snippet, the addition of card‑skimming functionality, and the deployment of iOS exploit routers. The attacker rebuilt the payload 26 times in a single day, adding features such as additional cryptocurrency wallets but never removing existing ones. By the end of the day the number of infected snippets fell from 169 to a single remaining snippet after a coordinated cleanup effort.

The payload, called track.js, performed several actions for every visitor. First, it searched the page, clipboard, form fields, links, images, fetch/XHR requests, window.open calls and the iOS share sheet for any valid cryptocurrency address (including Bitcoin, Ethereum, other EVM chains, TRON, Solana, TON, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash and Dogecoin) and replaced it with an attacker‑controlled address, preserving checksums to ensure only genuine addresses were swapped. Second, after 13:43 UTC, it began monitoring form submissions and POST requests for credit‑card numbers that passed the Luhn check, thereby enabling card skimming. Additional behaviors included cookie theft, screenshot capture and, on iOS devices, loading of the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits.

The article emphasizes that trusted third‑party JavaScript can become malicious without any breach of the target site’s own code or infrastructure. It argues that tools like Report URI, which detect unexpected changes to known scripts, new script loads and suspicious external connections, can expose such attacks. Moreover, implementing a strict Content‑Security‑Policy in enforcement mode could block key parts of the malicious payload even when it originates from a trusted domain. The incident illustrates the broader risk of supply‑chain compromises in web‑based services and the need for continuous monitoring and defensive policies.

stories.author: cwaffles
stories.title: Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use
stories.groq_label: Windows 11 MissionControlAggregator records and uploads usage of AI coding assistants and developer tools via optional diagnostic data
stories.groq_explain:
The article documents a reverse‑engineering investigation of a Windows 11 component called MissionControlAggregator.dll, which collects telemetry about the coding agents and developer tools a user runs. By opening the DLL in a disassembler the author identified hard‑coded executable names such as codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe, cursor.exe, as well as traditional development binaries like python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, clang.exe, javac.exe, devenv.exe, and code.exe. These names are used in a series of “executable‑name matcher” functions that compare running process identities against the list.

The component subscribes to existing Windows event streams rather than scanning processes directly. It listens to KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary and Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary for native Windows programs, and to Microsoft.Windows.Lxss.Manager.Exec and ExecCritical events for Linux processes running under WSL. When a match occurs, a slot in the component’s internal state is set.

Periodically the aggregator converts the set slots into bitfields representing twelve broad tool categories, four command‑line agents, and five desktop agents. It then emits an ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) self‑describing TraceLogging event named Segments.SubCohorts. The report contains only the bitmap of observed tools, along with timestamps for the collection window; detailed usage metrics such as duration or resource consumption are discarded.

The telemetry is stored locally and, unless the user has opted out of the optional diagnostic data (which is enabled by default), is uploaded to Microsoft via the DiagTrack (Connected User Experiences and Telemetry) service. The service runs automatically, launches an AggregatorHost.exe process, and loads MissionControlAggregator.dll. The author confirmed the feature was enabled on a Windows 11 ARM64 VM without manual configuration.

The significance of the finding lies in its privacy implications: Microsoft is silently tracking which AI coding assistants and development tools a user employs, potentially revealing sensitive information about a developer’s workflow and projects. This data collection occurs under the umbrella of optional diagnostics, which many users may not realize are active by default. The article provides detailed technical evidence of how the telemetry is gathered, processed, and transmitted.

stories.author: mfiguiere
stories.title: OpenCode Browse
stories.groq_label: OpenCode Browse enables AI agents to perform tasks inside a real web browser using existing tabs and logins.
stories.groq_explain:
OpenCode Browse is a product consisting of a Model Context Protocol server and a Chromium extension that enables artificial intelligence agents to interact directly with a user's local web browser. It is compatible with a wide range of Chromium-based browsers, including Chrome, Edge, Brave, Arc, Helium, Vivaldi, Opera, and general Chromium builds. By giving agents access to the user's active browser, agents can leverage existing web sessions and credentials without requiring complex setups or separate API keys.

The tool operates unobtrusively by running agent-driven tabs in the background inside collapsed tab groups. Agents can read web pages, click elements, type text, take screenshots, record tab sessions, and inspect network traffic. To protect user security, the system includes an allowed sites feature that restricts where agents can navigate. It also provides a handoff workflow for sensitive steps such as logins, two-factor authentication prompts, or payment processing, passing the tab back to the user and resuming action only after the user completes the step and clicks continue. Users can also manually hand over an open tab to an agent using a toolbar button.

OpenCode Browse works with any client supporting the Model Context Protocol, including OpenCode, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and Zed. Setup is designed to be straightforward by installing the Chrome extension first, though direct command line installation options using curl, PowerShell, npm, or bun are available. This product matters because it bridges the gap between AI development tools and real-world web environments, allowing automated web tasks while keeping sensitive credentials and session control in the hands of the user. The page also briefly mentions related developer tools, including Hex for on-device voice dictation, OpenTunnel for creating public HTTPS URLs for local applications, and OpenTUI for building terminal user interfaces.

Several additional courses are slated for release in January, such as “Probability and Computing,” “Multimodal Machine Learning,” “Product Management Essentials,” “AI and Machine Learning,” and “Requirements for Embedded Systems.”

An AI tutoring component is also in development to help learners work through questions. The platform invites viewers to subscribe on YouTube to stay updated with each new release. 

The effort is presented as a way to open Carnegie Mellon’s CS classroom to anyone who wishes to learn at their own pace, while also promoting the university’s reputation in cutting‑edge research areas. The site notes that the project is built by students with support from ScottyLabs, and it points to the option of enrolling as a full‑time student in the Kenneth C. Griffin School of Computer Science for those seeking a campus experience. stories.author: PaulHoule
stories.title: Grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays
stories.groq_label: Low-density sheep grazing around solar panels boosts beneficial insect populations and supports profitable agrivoltaic management.
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports on two recent Cornell research projects that examine the practice of grazing sheep in fields that host solar‑panel arrays, known as solar grazing or agrivoltaics. The first study, published in Environmental Research Letters, measured how different stocking rates of sheep affect beneficial insect populations. Researchers found that allowing two sheep per hectare increased the abundance of wild bees, honey bees and lady beetles by 38 percent compared with a mowed control, driven mainly by an 83 percent rise in honey‑bee numbers. When stocking was increased to four sheep per hectare, insect abundance returned to levels similar to the control but vegetation management improved. At eight sheep per hectare, vegetation control was maximized and flock health remained strong, yet honey‑bee numbers fell by 45 percent. The authors emphasize that stocking density is a concrete variable that farmers can use to balance insect benefits, vegetation management and animal health, providing a scientific basis for decision‑making by solar developers, municipalities and growers.

The second project, described in Manufacturing & Service Operations Management, presents a spreadsheet‑based decision‑support tool created by a team from Cornell’s Business and Engineering schools. The model helps sheep owners who graze on solar farms to optimize flock size, procurement, sales, cost structures and expected vegetation growth, while also aiding solar developers in designing contracts that are economically viable for both parties. The tool has already been adopted by United Agrivoltaics, a company that connects shepherds with solar‑farm operators.

Both studies highlight the broader potential of solar grazing to generate ecological benefits and new revenue streams for rural producers. By improving habitats for pollinators and offering a steady source of feed and income, solar grazing could help expand the domestic sheep industry, reduce reliance on imported lamb and stimulate related supply‑chain activities. The research suggests that integrating livestock management with renewable‑energy infrastructure can create synergistic outcomes for agriculture, biodiversity and the economy.

stories.author: burntsushi
stories.title: Jiff 1.0: A datetime library for Rust
stories.groq_label: Jiff 1.0 delivers a stable, timezone‑aware datetime library for Rust with a comprehensive API
stories.groq_explain:
Jiff is a Rust datetime library that has reached its 1.0 release and is positioned as a robust, ecosystem‑wide building block for handling dates, times, and time zones. The announcement emphasizes that Jiff places time‑zone handling at the core of its API, automatically managing many daylight‑saving‑time complexities, and that it has already been adopted by a number of high‑profile Rust projects such as Cargo, Starship, and Nushell. The author commits to maintaining the 1.0 API indefinitely unless a serious defect is discovered, noting that breaking changes would cause significant pain for downstream users.

The article explains the motivation behind Jiff, arguing that many datetime libraries expose too much complexity to users, whereas Jiff strives to encapsulate the difficult aspects of time handling. It introduces a shared vocabulary for the domain, defining civil time, UTC, TAI, leap seconds, and Unix time, and then describes the library’s “datetime onion” model. In this model a plain Gregorian date, a nanosecond‑precision clock time, and their combination as a civil DateTime are distinct from a Timestamp (nanoseconds since the Unix epoch) and from a TimeZone (rules for mapping between timestamps and civil datetimes). A ZonedDateTime ties together a timestamp, civil datetime, and time zone to represent an instant in a specific geographic location.

The post walks through how to create a ZonedDateTime in code, showing the creation of a civil date and time, combining them, and then applying a time‑zone identifier such as “America/New_York”. It also outlines the breadth of the library’s API, covering parsing and formatting with FromStr and Display, strptime/strftime style functions, locale‑sensitive formatting via ICU4X, duration handling with a “friendly” format, date arithmetic, rounding, span manipulation, and support for other calendar systems. The table of contents indicates sections on choosing the appropriate DateTime type, manipulation of dates and spans, and a conclusion that reinforces why developers should consider Jiff for convenient, correct datetime handling in Rust. The significance of the release lies in providing a stable, well‑designed foundation for time‑related functionality across the Rust ecosystem, reducing bugs related to daylight‑saving transitions and simplifying common datetime tasks.

stories.author: geerlingguy
stories.title: Frame – 31.5" color ePaper display
stories.groq_label: Full color 31.5 inch ePaper display in a handcrafted wooden frame now open for pre order with limited units shipping 2026 2027
stories.groq_explain:
The post announces the third product release from TRMNL, a 31.5‑inch full‑color ePaper display called Frame, which is housed in a handmade wooden enclosure. The device is now available for pre‑order, with an initial production run of roughly 470 units. The company expects to ship a few units by the end of 2026 and most deliveries in early 2027. A short promotional film is linked for more visual detail.

The announcement provides a brief history of the founder’s earlier venture, ArtSpot, which aimed to display local art in New York cafés and galleries but ultimately did not achieve sales despite easy artist recruitment and platform development. The experience shaped the creator’s ongoing interest in art and technology, leading to the development of the TRMNL line of ePaper devices.

Frame inherits the core features of other TRMNL products, such as displaying schedule, weather and artwork, but adds several new capabilities. Clock synchronization now allows updates at specific times of day rather than on a fixed interval, reducing screen flicker and extending battery life. An offline mode lets the device operate entirely from a microSD card without any internet connection, ensuring no personal data is sent to servers. Power is supplied by an internal rechargeable battery, and an optional second USB‑C port on the rear provides continuous connectivity for always‑on use.

A major technical advancement is the Lazarus color conversion engine, described as a high‑quality dithering and lookup‑table system that gives Frame the best color matching available for Spectra 6 displays. The software will be released as open source, allowing users to tune it themselves, and it will later be adapted for TRMNL’s four‑color devices.

Frame can be mounted in either portrait or landscape orientation without extra hardware, and a kickstand can be added if desired. The company is working with community developers to add Frame‑specific features, including a Local Art plugin that enables artists to submit and sell work directly through the TRMNL platform.

Production is largely kept in‑house to improve quality and control. The post lists the major components, their sourcing locations, lead times and current inventory levels. The 31.5‑inch ePaper panel, USB‑C cables, and PCBA assemblies are sourced overseas, while packaging, wooden bodies, plastic parts and fasteners are produced in the United States. Batteries, rigid foam and other items are also sourced internationally but stocked to reduce delays. All final assembly is performed by TRMNL staff rather than outsourced factories.

Logistics for the first batch are limited to the United States, Canada, Mexico and Australia, which are the regions the company’s U.S. warehouse currently ships to. Customers outside those areas may still order, but they must handle import duties and fees, and the option could be withdrawn if inventory runs out. The company also mentions plans to open a second woodworking shop near its future Berlin warehouse to support European distribution in 2027.

Overall, the announcement positions Frame as a novel, large‑format, full‑color ePaper device that blends art display with practical information, built with a transparent supply chain and a focus on in‑house manufacturing. The limited pre‑order run, open‑source color engine and integration with the TRMNL art marketplace are highlighted as the main reasons the product stands out in the ePaper market.

stories.author: luu
stories.title: Test/verification technique effectiveness with Astra
stories.groq_label: GPT-6 Astra demonstrates higher accuracy, cost efficiency, and effective use of testing techniques on programming tasks compared to GPT-5.6 Sol.
stories.groq_explain:
This article evaluates how effectively advanced AI language models use various software testing and verification techniques when implementing complex software tasks. It compares an older model generation, referred to as GPT-5.6 Sol, with a newer generation, GPT-6 Astra, across different programming benchmarks including implementations of Zstd, IMAP, and Pandoc specifications.

In earlier evaluations using GPT-5.6 Sol, asking the model to use specific testing techniques such as Test-Driven Development, QuickCheck, Lean 4, or fuzzing actually degraded performance compared to a default prompt that did not specify a testing methodology. Sol typically generated superficial or useless tests, such as ineffective random inputs during fuzzing, making default prompting the most effective option.

With GPT-6 Astra, the author observed two major changes. First, base capabilities improved drastically. On the Zstd implementation task, Astra achieved over 99 percent test correctness at medium effort for just one dollar per run, saturating the benchmark compared to Sol, which cost significantly more and achieved lower success rates. Second, Astra demonstrated a far better ability to meaningfully apply specialized testing techniques, such as generating structured fuzz tests that effectively explored code paths and identified non-trivial bugs.

To evaluate Astra on non-saturated tasks, the author ran tests on larger, more difficult specifications like IMAP and Pandoc. On the Pandoc evaluation, which required an average of 14 turns and cost roughly 90,000 dollars across 25 runs per condition, no technique reached 100 percent correctness. However, unlike with the older model, several specific testing and verification techniques outperformed the default prompt when measuring test correctness against cost.

While high evaluation costs limit the statistical certainty needed to explain every specific outcome, the results indicate that property-testing methods generally improve generalization on holdout tests relative to visible tests, whereas methods like TDD tend to show lower relative generalization. Overall, the findings suggest that as AI model capabilities progress to Astra's level, agents begin to derive genuine value from specialized testing and verification workflows rather than performing worse than default baseline prompts.

stories.author: zaik
stories.title: Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker
stories.groq_label: A malicious site can exploit uBlock Origin element picker to inject trusted filters and achieve universal XSS
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports a universal cross‑site scripting (UXSS) vulnerability discovered in the uBlock Origin extension for Firefox, specifically the Manifest V2 version, with a related but less severe problem in the Manifest V3 “uBO Lite” build. The flaw allows a malicious website to force the extension to add arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters are capable of injecting JavaScript into any page, so an attacker can execute code in the context of any site the victim visits.

The vulnerability stems from uBlock Origin’s element picker feature, which lets users block page elements via a right‑click menu. The picker is implemented by loading an internal iframe from a URL such as moz‑extension://<extension‑UUID>/web_accessible_resources/epicker‑ui.html. The iframe can communicate with the extension’s background script to add filter rules.

The attack proceeds in several stages. First, the attacker must discover the extension’s internal UUID, which is randomly generated per installation. This is possible because uBlock Origin ships with a default filter rule that hooks the fetch API (lootdest.*##+js(no-fetch-if, …)). The hook intercepts network requests for ad scripts and redirects them to a local script stored under the extension’s UUID. By overriding XMLHttpRequest.open, an attacker can detect when a request is made to a moz‑extension URL and read the UUID from the request URL.

With the UUID known, the attacker can embed the picker UI in a hidden iframe on their own page by setting the iframe’s src to the discovered internal URL. The attacker then opens a MessageChannel and sends a series of postMessage commands to the picker iframe, mimicking the normal picker workflow. By manipulating the “opt” field in a message that normally specifies the resource type (for example, image), the attacker can inject a newline and append a full trusted filter such as “google.com##+js(trusted‑rpnt, script, …)”. The picker does not validate the origin of these messages, allowing the malicious payload to be accepted.

Finally, the attacker can overlay or hide the iframe and trick the user into clicking the invisible “Create” button, causing the extension to add the attacker‑controlled trusted filter. Because filters added via the picker are automatically marked as trusted, they bypass normal safety checks. Even if the user later edits their custom filters, the attacker can act quickly by opening a target page before any recompilation clears the trusted status.

The article notes that a fix has been deployed. The remediation includes adding a secret token that the genuine element picker receives from the content script and must return in its initial postMessage, ensuring only legitimate pickers can accept commands. The author also credits GPT‑5.6 Sol for locating the issue and Claude for writing most of the proof‑of‑concept code.

The vulnerability matters because it demonstrates how a seemingly benign UI component of a popular ad‑blocking extension can be abused to gain script execution across arbitrary sites, effectively compromising the security model of the browser for any user of the affected extension. The fix restores the integrity of the element picker and prevents the injection of trusted filters from untrusted origins.

stories.author: aillia
stories.title: Tor Project Issues Rapid-Response DoS-Defense Fix Amid Sustained DDoS Attack
stories.groq_label: Tor Project released version 0.4.9.17 adding critical IPv6 DoS defense fixes and urges relay operators to upgrade during a sustained DDoS attack.
stories.groq_explain:
The page is an announcement from the Tor Project about a rapid‑response security release, version 0.4.9.17. The update contains a series of security fixes, with a particular emphasis on a fix that improves relay denial‑of‑service (DoS) defenses related to IPv6 handling. This release is being issued in direct response to an ongoing distributed denial‑of‑service (DDoS) attack that has been overwhelming many Tor relays with a flood of client circuits.

The announcement explains that the attack has affected most relay operators and that addressing the problem is difficult because the relays are being inundated with traffic. The Tor Project is actively evaluating additional defenses and expects further releases in the near future. Operators of Tor relays are urged to upgrade to the new version as soon as possible; no additional action is required after the upgrade.

The notice also thanks the relay operators and the tor‑relays@ mailing list for their support during the attack, while expressing frustration toward the attackers. The release notes reference the 0.4.9.x series and provide links for downloading tarballs, accessing the Gitlab repository, and viewing bug reports. The overall significance is that upgrading promptly will help protect the Tor network’s relays from the current DDoS pressure and improve overall security and stability.

stories.author: zdw
stories.title: What's Next for Nvidia?
stories.groq_label: Nvidia faces an uncertain future as it must replace Jensen Huang’s visionary leadership to sustain innovation.
stories.groq_explain:
The article discusses the implications of Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia after 33 years as its founder‑CEO. It frames the departure as a critical moment for a company whose success has been driven by Huang’s visionary leadership and multiple strategic reinventions. The piece outlines three major pivots Huang led: the 2006 launch of CUDA, which turned graphics chips into a general‑purpose computing platform; the 2012 shift toward deep learning after Nvidia’s GPUs helped win the ImageNet competition; and the 2020 acquisition of Mellanox, which moved the firm from selling individual GPU boards to providing integrated AI datacenter racks. Each pivot involved not just new products but entirely new business models, customer bases, and market channels.

The author argues that such transformative change requires a CEO who is both an entrepreneur and a deep technical understanding, comparing Huang to Steve Jobs. Visionary CEOs are described as the ones who anticipate market shifts, create new markets, and drive innovation rather than merely executing existing plans. The article then contrasts visionary leadership with execution‑focused CEOs, using Microsoft as a case study. Bill Gates’ hand‑off to Steve Ballmer resulted in strong financial performance but missed key trends in search, mobile, media and cloud, leading to a period of relative stagnation until Satya Nadella refocused the company on cloud computing and restored its relevance.

The piece further examines how visionary founders often do not plan for succession, leaving a vacuum that can be filled by executives who prioritize stability and process over innovation. It notes that Huang had about 60 direct reports, discouraged one‑on‑one meetings, and avoided formal succession planning, making the transition especially challenging. When an execution‑oriented CEO takes over, they typically add layers of management to impose order, which can suppress creative talent and lead to a “creative death spiral.” The article cites Apple under Tim Cook as an example where an execution leader managed to sustain growth and even introduce major technical change with Apple silicon, though it also hints at limits to such transitions.

Overall, the article warns that Nvidia faces a decisive crossroads: without a successor who can match Huang’s ability to envision and enact radical business model shifts, the company risks becoming a brand‑driven entity that coasts on past momentum rather than continuing to shape future markets. The author urges Nvidia’s board to consider these dynamics carefully as they search for new leadership. The text ends abruptly, cutting off during the discussion of Apple silicon, indicating the article may be incomplete.

stories.author: CharlesW
stories.title: Preserving 30 years of Salon journalism
stories.groq_label: Salon’s 31‑year archive of over 250,000 articles is accessible via the Wayback Machine and the new Salon Explorer
stories.groq_explain: The page announces that Salon, a pioneering online magazine launched in 1995, is ending its publication after more than three decades. Salon was among the first major publications created for the web, shaping digital journalism by mixing politics, culture, criticism and ideas for early internet readers. Although the site is closing, the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine has been continuously capturing its content since the late 1990s, preserving the site’s evolution through addresses such as salon1999.com, salonmag.com and salon.com. The archive now holds over 250,000 Salon articles, representing a substantial record of digital journalism and the cultural conversations that have taken place online since the web’s early days. To make this collection more accessible, the Archive has launched an experimental “Salon Explorer,” a new interface that lets users filter and browse the articles and the work of more than 20,000 writers. The effort matters because it safeguards a significant portion of internet‑age media history, ensuring that Salon’s contributions to online discourse remain available for research and public reference. The page provides links to the Salon Explorer and to browsing Salon.com directly in the Wayback Machine.

stories.author: hspeiser
stories.title: Old Bitly links are being hijacked
stories.groq_label: Bitly confirmed that bad actors are hijacking old inactive links to redirect users to unrelated or malicious content, leading to account suspensions and link disabling.
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports that Bitly has been allowing old, inactive short links to be re‑registered by malicious actors, causing them to redirect to unrelated or harmful content. Bitly confirmed the problem on X on 15 November 2026, saying it had identified the issue, suspended the accounts responsible and was disabling the affected links while its Trust and Safety team works on additional protections.

The story focuses on several high‑profile examples. A Bitly link in a Burger King tweet from 24 July 2011 was re‑created on 15 November 2026 and now points to Wikipedia’s list of Nazi concentration camps. A similar McDonald’s tweet from 7 June 2011 was re‑registered minutes earlier and redirects to the Wikipedia article on the September 11 attacks. Both links were later deactivated by Bitly, and the original tweets have become unavailable.

The investigation also examined 97 Bitly links used in Donald Trump’s tweets from 2009‑2013. Of those, 40 remain the original links, 49 were re‑created later but still point to the intended destinations, and seven now lead to unrelated destinations such as a Roblox profile, YouTube videos or a Wikipedia article about Trump and Jeffrey Epstein. Four of the seven were re‑registered on the same day as the Burger King incident and have since been disabled. One link is blocked by Bitly as malicious or spam.

Additional reports from CNN indicate that old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the U.S. Department of Defense have also been affected, though the article’s author did not verify those cases.

The article explains that Bitly’s public information page for each short URL shows the creation timestamp and destination. The fact that a link originally tweeted in 2011 now shows a 2026 creation date demonstrates that the same link suffix was issued a second time, contrary to Bitly’s claim that link endings cannot be reused after an account is deleted. Bitly had previously fixed a related bug in February 2025, but the new exploit appears to bypass that protection.

The piece concludes that the companies whose tweets were involved (Burger King, McDonald’s, Trump’s campaign, etc.) were not hacked; the compromise occurs on Bitly’s side, where the short links were taken over and repurposed. The incident matters because it shows a vulnerability in a widely used URL shortening service that can be abused to spread misinformation, extremist content, or malicious sites, and it raises concerns about the reliability of historic links that people may still click.
